title: Agents are Robots Too: What Self-Driving Taught Me About Building Agents — Jesse Hu, Abundant
talk_summary: A robotics/self-driving engineer draws analogies between autonomous vehicles and LLM agents, arguing that the model is only ~1% of the work and the rest is the 'offline stack' (simulation, logging, evaluation, closed-loop feedback). The concrete transferable ideas are closed-loop tool execution, treating agent runs as stateful, and hill-climbing via failure triage on logs rather than single benchmark scores.

takeaways.technique: Close the loop on long-running tool calls
takeaways.what_they_do: Instead of fire-and-forget bash/tool calls where the agent waits for the full response and cannot observe progress, they stream output and make execution observable so the agent can measure completion and exit early.
takeaways.evidence_quote: if I run a bash command and I run an open-ended process, well, sometimes I can't observe the outputs, at least not in real time

takeaways.what_they_do: Rather than trusting a single benchmark number, they break results down by category and triage individual failures to learn where to improve the system.
takeaways.evidence_quote: a 70% at a benchmark will tell you a little bit, but if you start to break them down into different categories

takeaways.what_they_do: Real-world deployment logs are fed back into the simulation engine to ground it, creating a full learn-deploy-log loop rather than one-shot evaluation.
takeaways.evidence_quote: once you deploy, you can actually get logs from the real world that feed back into your simulation engine

takeaways.technique: Treat agents as stateful, not stateless
takeaways.what_they_do: Moving from stateless sessions to stateful VMs with persistent file stores means you must reason about the whole world state an agent runs into, not just the single session artifact.
takeaways.evidence_quote: Now, we have VMs. VMs that are stateful both in terms of what's running, but also the persistent file store.

takeaways.what_they_do: Self-driving works because cars expose a predefined human control interface plus built-in telemetry, making actions and data collection codifiable; domains without that are much harder.
takeaways.evidence_quote: We have this predefined interface with predefined actions and predefined telemetry and that makes it much much easier of a task

takeaways.what_they_do: They argue input and action spaces are implicit design choices with tradeoffs; e.g. turn-based conversation is easy to reason about but cannot react to pop-ups or long-running processes in real time.
takeaways.evidence_quote: we don't do this thing that's natural robotics where we keep sampling from the world and we keep interacting in real time
